assessment.rationale: Strong wire-layer fit for opaque carriage: the minimal [pcid,payload] CBOR envelope lets lower layers store or forward condition references without parsing them, and unknown-pCID salvage is explicitly non-authoritative. Deterministic bytes and wrapper-selected signature protocols can support later verification. The main gap is that verification and promise accounting live outside the base envelope, so this specimen only partially answers end-to-end conditional-release evidence.
strengths: Clean layer split: lower layers carry opaque bytes while pCID-selected handlers own condition semantics.
Unknown-pCID policy marks salvage as unsupported/unverified, helping avoid accidental promise claims.
Deterministic CBOR bytes and wrapper signatures support stable hashing, signing, and later verification.
No central registry is required; new condition vocabularies can evolve behind new pCIDs.
weaknesses: The base envelope has no mandatory signature or condition-binding slot.
Peer-local promise-accounting records for store, release, or refusal are not defined here.
Audit quality depends heavily on having the relevant pCID handler.
The specimen is still draft and unfrozen.
risks: Operators may over-trust best-effort salvage output despite the unsupported/unverified warning.
If wrapper protocols are omitted or inconsistently used, opaque condition references may travel without strong binding to the encrypted object or signer.
open_questions: What concrete wrapper protocol binds a conditional-release or geofencing object to the encrypted content and signer identity?
What local records should Bob and Carol retain to prove safe carriage without semantic validation?
Should opaque conditional-release carriage require a minimal integrity wrapper even when semantics stay opaque?
assessment.authority_boundary: Evidence only; does not settle PromiseGrid design.
